clinicalPearls: An extremely rare, highly aggressive localised tumour of atypical mast cells with destructive growth
It presents as a solitary mass that invades and destroys local tissue
Despite an initially localised presentation, it has a strong tendency to disseminate
It may progress to a mast cell leukaemia-like picture
Diagnosis requires histology with mast cell markers and exclusion of systemic mastocytosis at presentation
Prognosis is poor, and management uses surgery, cytoreductive and targeted therapy with transplantation considered
reference.pathophysiology: Mast cell sarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of mast cells forming a destructive solid tumour, in contrast to the marrow-based infiltration of mast cell leukaemia. The atypical mast cells show high-grade cytological features and invade surrounding tissues. Although localised at diagnosis, the tumour behaves aggressively with a marked propensity for systemic spread, and terminal disease can resemble mast cell leukaemia. KIT and other mutations may be present and influence therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Anaplastic large cell or other lymphoma
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy with mast cell immunohistochemistry
Staging imaging for local extent and dissemination
redFlags: Rapid local growth and tissue destruction
reference.prognosis: Mast cell sarcoma has a poor prognosis with frequent dissemination and progression despite treatment, although outcomes may improve with targeted therapy and transplantation in selected cases.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a benign extracutaneous mastocytoma
Delaying molecular characterisation that could guide targeted therapy
Failing to assess for systemic mast cell disease
management: Complete surgical resection of the localised destructive tumour where feasible
Local radiotherapy for unresectable or residual disease
KIT-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors and cytoreductive therapy, guided by mutation analysis, given the strong tendency to disseminate
Consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in selected patients
Mediator-directed therapy with antihistamines and self-injectable adrenaline for mediator release and anaphylaxis
Surveillance for systemic dissemination and progression to a mast cell leukaemia-like picture
Coordinate management through a specialist multidisciplinary sarcoma and haematology team
